name: Ganoderma lucidum (Reishi / Lingzhi)

lead: Reishi or lingzhi is a woody mushroom used for over two thousand years in East Asian medicine. People take it for immunity, relaxation and sleep, hoping better rest and lower stress show up as a fresher look and better skin.

Polysaccharides and triterpenes are thought to be the active constituents, with immune-modulating and antioxidant effects reported in cell and animal studies. A Cochrane review cited by Wikipedia found no good clinical evidence for cardiovascular or other medical uses owing to poor-quality research, and no trial has tested it for appearance.

paras: It is taken as tea, extract or capsules, often in the evening for winding down, or daily as an immune tonic. Users treat it as a long-term routine alongside sleep and recovery habits.

Wikipedia reports safety concerns and moderate interactions with some medicines and supplements. Product identity varies: DNA testing found many items labelled G. lucidum contained other species. It is sold as a supplement.

web.title: Reishi Mushroom - Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center

angle.text: Reishi is taken as tea or extract for immunity, stress and sleep: calmer evenings and better rest are hoped to show up as a fresher look and better skin. Clinical research on sleep and immunity is limited.

lead: Ganoderma lucidum, known as reishi in Japan and lingzhi in China, is a glossy, woody bracket fungus used for centuries in traditional East Asian medicine, where it was regarded as a health and longevity mushroom.[1][2][3] It is taken as tea, extract, capsules or spore oil, and in wellness and recovery circles it is used as a calming, immune-supporting and sleep-supporting supplement. People who use it this way connect it to appearance through a chain: calmer evenings and better sleep, lower perceived stress and steadier recovery, which then feed into training consistency and a rested look.

Reishi also appears in skincare and nutrition writing. A 2021 review titled as covering the mushroom's nutritional, cosmeceutical, mycochemical, pharmacological, clinical and toxicological properties describes cosmeceutical value alongside medical uses, and lists its polysaccharides, triterpenoids, sterols, proteins and nucleosides.[4]

Its taxonomy is unsettled: many products and grow kits labelled G. lucidum have been found to contain other species such as G. sichuanense (G. lingzhi).[5][6] Reviews describe polysaccharides and triterpenes as principal bioactive constituents and report immunomodulatory and anticancer effects mainly in cell and animal work.[1][3][7][8] A Cochrane review cited by Wikipedia concluded that, owing to poor-quality clinical research, good evidence is lacking for use in cardiovascular risk or other conditions.[5] Trials examining sleep, stress, immune function and blood lipids exist and are summarised below; no trial of reishi for appearance outcomes was identified.

Beyond supplements, lingzhi has a long cultural life as an emblem of health and longevity in Chinese art and Taoist tradition, often called the mushroom of immortality [9]. Modern wellness culture folds it into adaptogen-style routines, tonics and mushroom blends, a category whose label the US FDA has addressed in warning letters to supplement makers [10].
infobox: Reishi, lingzhi, varnished conk, Ganoderma lucidum / G. lingzhi[5]
Chinese, Japanese, Korean medicine for over 2,000 years[2]
Tea, dried extract, capsules, spore powder and oil[14]

paras: Wikipedia describes G. lucidum as a red-to-purple-brown species with a shiny, fan-shaped cap that can reach 35 cm across and a long stalk, growing on decaying stumps, mainly plum or oak. The genus and species names derive from Greek and Latin roots for sheen and brightness.[5] Dried, it is hard and inedible but is used to brew a bitter tea.[5] It is cultivated intensively in Japan, Korea and China and grown in some South American countries.[5]

In Chinese, the name língzhī combines words for spirit or divine and for mushroom, so it is often translated as divine mushroom; reishi is the Japanese reading, and related names include yeongji in Korean and linh chi in Vietnamese [9]. Since the early 1970s most lingzhi has been grown on hardwood logs, sawdust, woodchips or grain, and shape features such as stem length and antler-like forms respond to light, temperature, humidity and carbon dioxide levels [9].

The genus name was applied by Karsten in 1881, and the species had earlier been described as Boletus lucidus.[5] Molecular studies show G. lucidum is not closely related to G. sichuanense, the species often cultivated in Asia as lingzhi, and global phylogenetic work describes a complex of many species.[5][6]
One DNA-based survey reported by Wikipedia found that most grow-your-own kits and about half of dried products labelled G. lucidum actually contained G. sichuanense.[5]

Wikipedia also reports that in one DNA study no manufactured reishi product contained G. lucidum itself and that other species found in products included G. applanatum, G. australe, G. gibbosum, G. sessile and G. sinense.[5]

Wikipedia's lingzhi article reports that which Ganoderma species is the true lingzhi was still debated as of 2023, that G. lingzhi has been treated as a synonym of G. sichuanense, and that the older name G. lucidum persists in popular use although Asian and European populations are now considered distinct [9]. A 2018 DNA study discussed in Wikipedia's G. lucidum article found 93 per cent of grow-your-own kits and half of the dried products labelled G. lucidum contained G. sichuanense [5].

Reviews list polysaccharides, triterpenoids, alkaloids and sterols among the constituents, with reported antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, antiviral and immunomodulating activity in laboratory studies.[1][3][8][11] Analytical methods for the active components are an area of active work.[12]

The main compounds include triterpenes called ganoderic acids, whose structures resemble those of steroid hormones, and polysaccharides such as beta-glucans, along with sterols, alkaloids, coumarin and mannitol [9]. Memorial Sloan Kettering names beta-glucans and triterpenes as the active components and reports laboratory and animal findings of immune modulation and cancer-preventive effects [13]. Traditional preparation is a hot-water extract simmered for about two hours, which is bitter; modern products include tablets, capsules, powders, teas, soups and processed mycelia or spores [9].

Reviews describe lingzhi as a species revered for treating assorted diseases and prolonging life, used for more than two thousand years in Chinese, Japanese and Korean traditions.[2][3] Its Western taxonomic history begins with Curtis's 1781 description as Boletus lucidus and Karsten's 1881 genus Ganoderma; Patouillard's 1889 monograph placed 48 species in the genus.[5] Reviews note that its distribution across many regions has contributed to confusion about which species is meant.[2]

Wikipedia's lingzhi article says it has been revered for over 2,000 years, notes some evidence of use in Neolithic China about 6,800 years ago, and links early texts to Taoist ideas of immortality, with practitioners associating it with spiritual visions and transcendence [9]. The Shennong bencao jing sorted zhi mushrooms into six colours, each tied to a different organ, and in Chinese art lingzhi symbolises health and longevity and appears in imperial palaces; the bodhisattva Guanyin is sometimes shown holding one [9].

Reishi is taken as tea or decoction, powdered fruiting-body or mycelium extract, capsules, tinctures, spore powder and spore oil, and increasingly as a component of mushroom blends sold for evening or relaxation routines [9][14]. In recovery and wellness circles it is placed alongside other tonic herbs; the appearance logic proponents give runs through sleep and stress: calmer evenings, more consistent sleep and recovery, steadier training and a rested complexion [15].

Skincare is a second pathway. A 2021 comprehensive review of reishi covers cosmeceutical properties alongside nutritional, pharmacological and clinical ones [4]. No published human trial has tested reishi for skin, hair or body-composition outcomes.

Mushroom supplements are marketed for many health purposes, and Wikipedia's medicinal mushroom article states that product quality can vary because of inconsistent processing and labelling [16]. The adaptogen concept, coined in 1947 by the Soviet toxicologist Nikolai Lazarev, is described on Wikipedia as vaguely defined and not accepted as a marketing term in the EU or US, and between 2020 and 2023 the FDA issued warning letters to supplement makers over claims about adaptogen products, including a 2020 letter saying a mushroom supplement maker's products were being marketed as unapproved new drugs [10].

Memorial Sloan Kettering lists purported uses including immune support, strength and stamina, lowering cholesterol and relief of lower urinary tract symptoms in men, and notes that statements about supplements have not been evaluated by the FDA [13]. Within looksmaxxing and lifting communities the mushroom appears mainly as one of several tonic or adaptogen ingredients rather than as a topic of its own [15].

A review of anticancer evidence noted that research is predominantly in vitro and in vivo, and called it debatable whether lingzhi is a supplement or a therapy.[7] A study in patients with advanced colorectal cancer monitored immune responses to a Ganoderma preparation.[17]

ClinicalTrials.gov lists registered trials in cancer in children (Phase 3, n=58), Parkinson's disease (Phase 2, n=360; Phase 3, n=288), rheumatoid arthritis (Phase 2, n=70), fatty liver disease, sleep quality and chronic fatigue, with several recruiting or of unknown status.[18][19][20][21] Results are not summarised in the registry entries cited here. No studies on skin, hair, face or body appearance were found.

Several randomized trials exist. A 12-week double-blind trial of G. lucidum spore oil in 110 people with dyslipidemia reported lower total cholesterol, triglycerides and LDL-C and higher HDL-C than placebo, with improved liver function markers.[14] A double-blind trial in sedentary female college students tested 500 mg and 1000 mg daily doses of reishi against placebo for psychological stress and selected fitness parameters.[22] A 2024 randomized trial reported that a dry extract modulated T lymphocyte function in older women,[23] and a 2007 trial examined safety and tolerability in healthy subjects.[24] Memorial Sloan Kettering lists small trials suggesting benefit for urinary symptoms in men, while randomized trials did not support use for cardiovascular risk factors in type 2 diabetes.[13]

Memorial Sloan Kettering summarises clinical findings including possible benefit for urinary symptoms in men, mild antidiabetic effects, improved lipids and reduced anxiety, while randomised trials did not support reduced cardiovascular risk in type 2 diabetes, no effect was seen in fibromyalgia and a pilot study in Alzheimer's disease did not help [13]. Small cancer studies reported higher antioxidant capacity and immune and tumour responses, and the same page says more research is needed [13]. A Cochrane review by Klupp and colleagues (2015, updated 2021) found no good evidence for use in cardiovascular disease in people with type 2 diabetes or other conditions [5].

Wikipedia reports safety concerns and moderate interactions with some medicines and supplements.[5] Memorial Sloan Kettering lists nausea, insomnia, dry mouth, constipation, itching and vertigo as commonly reported effects, and describes case reports of liver toxicity with powdered reishi, including one fatal case.[13]

The same source notes theoretical interactions with anticoagulant and antiplatelet drugs (bleeding risk) and immunosuppressants, laboratory inhibition of several CYP450 enzymes of unknown clinical relevance, possible prolongation of clotting tests, and a suggestion that immunostimulatory effects may worsen autoimmune skin disease, though causation is not established.[13] It also reports that reishi spore powder may raise the tumour marker CA72-4.[13]

Memorial Sloan Kettering also describes case reports of chronic diarrhoea in a man with lymphoma, raised eosinophils with liver nodules that resolved after reishi was stopped, and acute neurotoxicity in a child who took several medicinal fungi at once, and advises talking with health providers before taking reishi [13]. The same page notes that one extract was toxic to white blood cells in laboratory work [13]. Because product identity is variable, the species and part of the mushroom in a given product can differ from its label [5].

sections.h: Use in recovery and wellness communities
paras: Reishi appears in adaptogen and sleep-support stacks. On T Nation forums, lifters mention it among tonic herbs and mushrooms (alongside lion's mane and cordyceps) taken for gut health, mood and nerve recovery, with some users describing themselves as strong believers and others noting that herbs can interact with each other.[15] Claims centre on relaxation, immunity and sleep; users link these to recovery, with a link to appearance through rest and training consistency.

lore.intro: Reishi is discussed as a calming, immune-supporting mushroom in wellness and lifting stacks, and as a longevity symbol in East Asian tradition [15][9].
